## Hardware abstraction (`hal/`)

The chip: registers, the timer, USB controller, flash, PWM, power. Nothing here knows what a keyboard is.

### `hal/clock.h`

#### `clock_init`

```c
void clock_init(void);
```

Switches the system clock to the PLL (24 MHz). First thing after reset.

#### `clock_wake_restart`

```c
void clock_wake_restart(void);
```

After a power-down: the oscillator and the PLL start again. The PLL's "locked" flag trips before a cold oscillator is stable enough for USB, so this settles by a delay instead.

#### `clock_stop`

```c
void clock_stop(void);
```

Stops the PLL and the oscillator, for a power-down.

### `hal/delay.h`

#### `delay_us`

```c
void delay_us(uint8_t us);
```

Busy-wait delays, calibrated for the 24 MHz clock (see delay.c). Not exact: for settling times, not for timing signals.

#### `delay_ms`

```c
void delay_ms(uint16_t ms);
```

#### `delay_us_nokick`

```c
void delay_us_nokick(uint8_t us);
```

delay_us() kicks the watchdog while it waits (see delay.c); this one does not, for code that runs in an interrupt.

### `hal/flash.h`

The chip's program flash, read and written by the application itself (IAP, through the SSP registers). Only the area from FLASH_WRITE_MIN to FLASH_WRITE_MAX can be changed: the application below it and the bootloader above it are never touched, whatever address a caller passes.

```c
#define FLASH_SECTOR_SIZE 512u
#define FLASH_WRITE_MIN   0xDC00u  // the application ends here: the keymap store, the settings and the bootloader's marker follow
#define FLASH_WRITE_MAX   0xF000u  // the stock bootloader starts here
```

#### `flash_read`

```c
void flash_read(uint16_t addr, uint8_t *dst, uint8_t len);
```

#### `flash_erase_sector`

```c
bool flash_erase_sector(uint16_t addr);
```

Erases the sector that holds `addr`. False (and nothing happens) if it is outside the writable area.

#### `flash_program`

```c
bool flash_program(uint16_t addr, const uint8_t *src, uint8_t len);
```

Programs bytes in erased cells. False (and nothing happens) if the range is outside the writable area.

### `hal/gpio.h`

#### `GPIO_DIR_WRITE`

```c
#define GPIO_DIR_WRITE(port, value)    (P##port##CR = (uint8_t)(value))
```

`port` is the port number (0-7), pasted into the register name: GPIO_HIGH(6, 0x03) sets P6 bits 0 and 1.

1 = output

```c
#define GPIO_PULLUP_WRITE(port, value) (P##port##PCR = (uint8_t)(value))  // 1 = pull-up on
#define GPIO_WRITE(port, value)        (P##port = (uint8_t)(value))
#define GPIO_HIGH(port, mask)          (P##port |= (uint8_t)(mask))
#define GPIO_LOW(port, mask)           (P##port &= (uint8_t) ~(mask))
#define GPIO_OUTPUT(port, mask)        (P##port##CR |= (uint8_t)(mask))
#define GPIO_INPUT(port, mask)         (P##port##CR &= (uint8_t) ~(mask))
#define GPIO_PULLUP_ON(port, mask)     (P##port##PCR |= (uint8_t)(mask))
#define GPIO_PULLUP_OFF(port, mask)    (P##port##PCR &= (uint8_t) ~(mask))
```

### `hal/power.h`

Power-down of the SH68F90A. The caller must arm a wake-up source first (power_wake_arm), or the core never comes back.

The handler is declared here because SDCC builds the vector table from the module that defines main(): main.c must include this header.

#### `power_int4_isr`

```c
void power_int4_isr(void) __interrupt(1);
```

INT_INT4

#### `power_wake_arm`

```c
void power_wake_arm(void);
```

INT4 as the wake-up source, with the values the stock firmware writes; and off again.

#### `power_wake_disable`

```c
void power_wake_disable(void);
```

#### `power_enter_powerdown`

```c
void power_enter_powerdown(void);
```

Stops the USB controller, the clock and the regulator and halts the core until INT4 (or a USB event) wakes it; then restarts the clock and the regulator. The caller starts USB again.

### `hal/pwm.h`

The 18 PWM channels of the SH68F90A: three banks of six (PWM0x, PWM1x, PWM2x) with a shared period each, and per channel a control register and two duty registers, 16 bits each (low and high byte in two places). They sit in XDATA at 0xFF80 and up; channel `k` is bank * 6 + number. The output is high between DUTY1 and DUTY2, whichever is the larger (checked with the LED probe, docs/keyboards/yunzii-b68.md), so DUTY2 - DUTY1 is the width.

```c
#define PWM_CHANNELS 18
#define PWM_REG(address, k) (*(__xdata volatile uint8_t *)((address) + (k)))
#define PWM_CON(k)    PWM_REG(0xFF80u, k)
#define PWM_DUTY1L(k) PWM_REG(0xFFA0u, k)
#define PWM_DUTY1H(k) PWM_REG(0xFFB8u, k)
#define PWM_DUTY2L(k) PWM_REG(0xFFD0u, k)
#define PWM_DUTY2H(k) PWM_REG(0xFFE8u, k)
```

#### `PWM_PERDL`

```c
#define PWM_PERDL(b) PWM_REG(0xFF98u, b)
```

The period of bank b (0-2)

```c
#define PWM_PERDH(b) PWM_REG(0xFF9Cu, b)
#define PWM_CON_BANK_ON    0x89  // the first channel of a bank starts the bank (the values the stock firmware writes)
#define PWM_CON_CHANNEL_ON 0x08
#define PWM_CON_OFF        0x00
```

### `hal/tick.h`

Timer 2 drives the whole timing of the keyboard: it plays the slots of core/sched.h (an LED subframe, or a scan of the key matrix) and counts milliseconds from the time that really passes. Each interrupt restarts the timer for the slot that begins, as the SMK port does, so a long scan never cuts the LED slot after it short.

The handler is declared here because SDCC builds the vector table from the module that defines main(): main.c must include this header.

#### `tick_isr`

```c
void tick_isr(void) __interrupt(0);
```

INT_TIMER2

#### `tick_hook_scan`

```c
void tick_hook_scan(uint8_t raw[16]);
```

Provided by the board: the work of the two kinds of slots. They run inside the interrupt and are timed from the start of their own interrupt (core/sched.h).

scan the key matrix: raw[col] has bit `row` set for a pressed key

#### `tick_hook_led`

```c
void tick_hook_led(bool give_up);
```

play one subframe of the backlight; `give_up`: the timer is running late, switch the backlight off instead

#### `tick_init`

```c
void tick_init(void);
```

#### `tick_pause`

```c
void tick_pause(void);
```

Stops / restarts the slots (around a flash write, which blocks interrupts for milliseconds).

#### `tick_resume`

```c
void tick_resume(void);
```

#### `tick_take`

```c
bool tick_take(void);
```

True once for every millisecond that has passed and has not been taken.

#### `tick_scan_take`

```c
bool tick_scan_take(uint8_t raw[16]);
```

True once for every scan of the matrix not yet taken; its result is copied to `raw`.

#### `tick_count_now`

```c
uint16_t tick_count_now(void);
```

The timer's count right now (the erase in a flash write is the only user: it is the clock that keeps running when the interrupt is off).

#### `tick_alive`

```c
void tick_alive(void);
```

The main loop calls this once per pass. The timer interrupt watches it: if the main loop has not come round for a few scans, the interrupt work does not fit its slots and is starving it, and the backlight steps aside (see tick.c) so that the keys, USB and the watchdog get the CPU.

### `hal/usb.h`

The USB device controller of the SH68F90A: the chip side of core/usb_device (EP0), core/usb_reports (EP1 IN) and, later, the raw HID pipe (EP2).

The handler is declared here because SDCC builds the vector table from the module that defines main(): main.c must include this header.

#### `usb_isr`

```c
void usb_isr(void) __interrupt(7);
```

INT_USB

#### `usb_hw_init`

```c
void usb_hw_init(void);
```

Powers the transceiver and connects to the bus. After the clock is on the PLL, with the interrupts still off.

#### `usb_hw_take_event`

```c
bool usb_hw_take_event(void);
```

True once after a bus reset or a new configuration: whatever the main loop had queued for the host is stale.

#### `usb_hw_suspended`

```c
bool usb_hw_suspended(void);
```

The bus is suspended (no start-of-frame for a while).

#### `usb_hw_wake_host`

```c
void usb_hw_wake_host(bool on);
```

Drives the resume signalling on the bus (USBCON.WKUP, the remote wakeup): on = start, off = end. The host must have suspended the bus and enabled the device's remote wakeup. The stock firmware sets this bit when a key wakes the chip while the host is suspended (0x9D73, 0x7F11).

#### `usb_hw_setup_seen`

```c
bool usb_hw_setup_seen(void);
```

The host has sent at least one SETUP packet since power-on: something is driving the bus.

#### `usb_hw_deinit`

```c
void usb_hw_deinit(void);
```

Disconnects from the bus and switches the controller off, for a power-down.

### `hal/watchdog.h`

Writing RSTSTAT kicks the watchdog. Compiled in only with -DWATCHDOG_ENABLE, so a build that does not use it never touches the register.

```c
#    define watchdog_kick() (RSTSTAT = WATCHDOG_PERIOD)
#    define watchdog_kick() ((void)0)
```

## Core logic (`core/`)

Hardware-independent C, tested on the host with gcc. It reaches the hardware only through `*_hook_*` functions that the board (or a test) provides.

### `core/combo.h`

Combos: two or more keys pressed together give one other key (Vial's Combos tab edits them, core/keymap.c stores them). The entries are keycodes, not positions: a combo fires when every one of its inputs is down within COMBO_TERM_MS of the first one.

The keys of a chord must not reach the host on their own, or "j" + "k" would type "jk" and then Escape. So a key that is an input of a configured combo is held back for at most COMBO_TERM_MS: if the chord completes, the held keys are dropped and the output is pressed (and released when they are let go); if the term passes, the held keys go out as if nothing had happened. A key that is not an input of any combo flushes what is held and goes through at once, so ordinary typing pays nothing.

This is the simple half of QMK's combo engine: exact matches only (the inputs of a combo, all of them and no more), one chord at a time, no overlapping chords.

```c
#define COMBO_TERM_MS 50u  // how long the keys are held back waiting for the rest of the chord (QMK's default)
```

#### `combo_init`

```c
void combo_init(void);
```

#### `combo_process`

```c
bool combo_process(uint8_t row, uint8_t col, uint16_t keycode, bool pressed, uint16_t now);
```

A key of the matrix went down or up, with the keycode it resolved to. True when the combo engine took the event (it is holding the key back, swallowed it, or turned it into a combo): in that case the caller must not act on the keycode.

#### `combo_task`

```c
void combo_task(uint16_t now);
```

Regularly from the main loop: the keys held back go out once the term has passed.

#### `combo_hook_send`

```c
void combo_hook_send(uint16_t keycode, bool pressed);
```

Provided by the caller: press or release a keycode on the host.

### `core/diag.h`

Counters for the first runs on the hardware, read over the raw HID interface (VIA command 0xF1, no unlock needed: they are read-only; tools/diag.py prints them). They are there to answer questions the host tests cannot: did the chip reset and why, how deep did the stack go, did the timer slots fit in their time, did the main loop stall.

Each counter has one writer (an interrupt or the main loop), so none needs a lock; a 16-bit value is read twice until it agrees.

#### `diag_id_t`

```c
typedef enum {
    DIAG_RESET_CAUSE,      // RSTSTAT as read at power-on, before the first watchdog kick
    DIAG_STACK_USED,       // bytes of the stack used at most (internal RAM from 0x21 up)
    DIAG_SLOT_LATE,        // LED slots whose work ran past their end (the timer had already overflowed again)
    DIAG_LOOP_MAX_MS,      // the slowest pass of the main loop
    DIAG_USB_OVERFLOW,     // USB report packets that replaced or pushed out another
    DIAG_BACKOFF,          // times the main loop was found starved and the backlight stood aside
    DIAG_SCAN_LATE,        // the same as DIAG_SLOT_LATE, for the scan slots
    DIAG_ERASE_US_MAX,     // the longest sector erase of a flash write, in us (the chip stalls while it runs)
    DIAG_RADIO_RX,         // frames from the radio that passed the checksum
    DIAG_TIMER_LATE_US,    // the longest the timer interrupt waited to start after its slot ended, in us (another interrupt or the flash holding it up; ignores the
                           // flash pauses, over 1 ms): above ~50 the backlight columns show it as a flicker
    DIAG_USB_GONE,         // times the keyboard declared the host gone (no start-of-frame in a look at the bus): with the cable in and the PC on this stays 0
    DIAG_STORE_SAVES,      // times the whole keymap has been written to flash, ever (the sequence number in the header of the slot in use: it survives power-off)
    DIAG_STORE_LOG,        // records in the log of the slot in use (the keymap edits written since the last whole save)
    DIAG_COUNT
} diag_id_t;
```

#### `diag_hook_refresh`

```c
void diag_hook_refresh(void);
```

Provided by the board: bring the counters that are read from somewhere else (stack, USB queue, matrix) up to date.

#### `diag_init`

```c
void     diag_init(void);
```

#### `diag_set`

```c
void     diag_set(diag_id_t id, uint16_t value);
```

#### `diag_inc`

```c
void     diag_inc(diag_id_t id);
```

saturates

#### `diag_max`

```c
void     diag_max(diag_id_t id, uint16_t value);
```

#### `diag_get`

```c
uint16_t diag_get(diag_id_t id);
```

#### `diag_receive`

```c
void diag_receive(XDATA uint8_t *data, uint8_t length);
```

VIA command 0xF1: the request is in `data` (32 bytes) and becomes the reply. [0xF1, kind, ...] kind 0: [0xF1, 0, DIAG_COUNT, counter 0 (lo, hi), counter 1, ...] kind 1: the radio: [0xF1, 1, its 6 status bytes] (the battery reading is in bytes 4-5) both are read-only, so they need no unlock anything else: [0xFF, ...] (unhandled)

#### `diag_hook_radio_status`

```c
const uint8_t *diag_hook_radio_status(void);
```

Provided by the board: the radio's last status bytes (6), for kind 1 (null until the first answer)

### `core/encoder.h`

Rotary encoders read as two lines in quadrature. The pins step through the Gray code 0 -> 1 -> 3 -> 2 -> 0 one way (clockwise) and the reverse the other way; a detent is a whole cycle of four steps. A jump of two states is a missed sample and counts for nothing, and a contact that bounces forward and back cancels out.

```c
#define ENCODER_RESOLUTION 4  // state changes per detent
```

#### `encoder_hook_state`

```c
uint8_t encoder_hook_state(uint8_t index);
```

Provided by the board (or a test): the two lines of encoder `index`, bit 0 = A, bit 1 = B.

#### `encoder_init`

```c
void encoder_init(void);
```

#### `encoder_poll`

```c
void encoder_poll(void);
```

Reads the lines of every encoder: call at every scan of the matrix.

#### `encoder_next`

```c
bool encoder_next(uint8_t index, bool *clockwise);
```

Takes one detent that has not been used yet. False when there is none.

### `core/hud.h`

The keyboard HUD protocol: lets a desktop overlay show the keyboard's live state (layers, pressed keys, modifiers, lock LEDs). It rides on the VIA / Vial raw HID interface as command 0xF0 and only ever answers requests: nothing is sent unasked and nothing is stored. The description is in docs/hud-protocol-v2.md; the B68 has 16 columns, so it announces protocol 2.

Every packet is 32 bytes: [0xF0, command, status, sequence, args... / reply...]; multi-byte fields are little-endian. 0x01 GET_INFO    protocol, rows, columns, layers, capability bits, HUD_TOG keycode, keymap version, bytes per row 0x02 GET_STATE   layer mask, default layer, pressed keys (the first 8 columns), mods, one-shots, flags, toggle counter, keymap version 0x03 GET_KEYMAP  args: layer, offset (16 bit, row * columns + column), count (<= 12); reply: the keycodes 0x04 GET_MATRIX  (protocol 2) the whole pressed-key matrix, rows * ceil(columns / 8) bytes

```c
#define HUD_CMD 0xF0u
```

#### `HUD_TOGGLE_KEYCODE`

```c
#define HUD_TOGGLE_KEYCODE 0x7E00u
```

The keycode of the HUD_TOG key (the first of the board's own keycodes); its presses are counted, not sent to the host.

#### `hud_hook_host_leds`

```c
uint8_t hud_hook_host_leds(void);
```

Provided by the board (or a test): the LED report of the host (bit 0 num lock, bit 1 caps lock).

#### `hud_receive`

```c
bool hud_receive(XDATA uint8_t *data, uint8_t length);
```

Handles a request in `data` (32 bytes) and turns it into the reply. False if `data` is not a HUD packet.

#### `hud_toggle_pressed`

```c
void hud_toggle_pressed(void);
```

The HUD_TOG key went down: the overlay sees the counter change.

Glue between the matrix events and the logic behind them: layers now, tapping, report and macros as they are added.


#### `keyboard_tap`

A tap of a keycode, as if a key of the keymap had gone down and up (used by the Leader's sequences).

True while Caps Word is on (the letters are being shifted until the word ends): the HUD and the diagnostics can show it.

#### `keyboard_hook_activity`

```c
void keyboard_hook_activity(void);
```

Provided by the board: a key changed or the knob turned (the keyboard is in use).

### `core/keycodes.h`

16-bit keycodes, laid out as QMK/Vial does: the Vial desktop app edits the keymap with these numbers, so the ranges cannot change. Only what Oblio uses is defined here.

#### `QK_BASIC`

```c
#define QK_BASIC              0x0000u
```

---- ranges ----

```c
#define QK_BASIC_MAX          0x00FFu
#define QK_MODS               0x0100u  // modifiers + a basic key, e.g. LSFT(KC_A)
#define QK_MODS_MAX           0x1FFFu
#define QK_MOD_TAP            0x2000u
#define QK_MOD_TAP_MAX        0x3FFFu
#define QK_LAYER_TAP          0x4000u
#define QK_LAYER_TAP_MAX      0x4FFFu
#define QK_LAYER_MOD          0x5000u
#define QK_LAYER_MOD_MAX      0x51FFu
#define QK_TO                 0x5200u
#define QK_TO_MAX             0x521Fu
#define QK_MOMENTARY          0x5220u
#define QK_MOMENTARY_MAX      0x523Fu
#define QK_DEF_LAYER          0x5240u
#define QK_DEF_LAYER_MAX      0x525Fu
#define QK_TOGGLE_LAYER       0x5260u
#define QK_TOGGLE_LAYER_MAX   0x527Fu
#define QK_ONE_SHOT_LAYER     0x5280u
#define QK_ONE_SHOT_LAYER_MAX 0x529Fu
#define QK_ONE_SHOT_MOD       0x52A0u
#define QK_ONE_SHOT_MOD_MAX   0x52BFu
#define QK_LAYER_TAP_TOGGLE   0x52C0u
#define QK_LAYER_TAP_TOGGLE_MAX 0x52DFu
#define QK_TAP_DANCE          0x5700u
#define QK_TAP_DANCE_MAX      0x57FFu
#define QK_MACRO              0x7700u
#define QK_MACRO_MAX          0x777Fu
#define QK_CAPS_WORD_TOGGLE   0x7C73u  // QMK's Caps Word: the next letters are shifted until the word ends
#define QK_LEADER             0x7C58u  // QMK's Leader: the keys after it are a sequence, not typing
#define QK_KB                 0x7E00u  // keyboard-specific keycodes
#define QK_KB_MAX             0x7E3Fu
#define IN_RANGE(code, lo, hi) ((code) >= (lo) && (code) <= (hi))
#define IS_QK_BASIC(code)           IN_RANGE(code, QK_BASIC, QK_BASIC_MAX)
#define IS_QK_MODS(code)            IN_RANGE(code, QK_MODS, QK_MODS_MAX)
#define IS_QK_MOD_TAP(code)         IN_RANGE(code, QK_MOD_TAP, QK_MOD_TAP_MAX)
#define IS_QK_LAYER_TAP(code)       IN_RANGE(code, QK_LAYER_TAP, QK_LAYER_TAP_MAX)
#define IS_QK_LAYER_MOD(code)       IN_RANGE(code, QK_LAYER_MOD, QK_LAYER_MOD_MAX)
#define IS_QK_TO(code)              IN_RANGE(code, QK_TO, QK_TO_MAX)
#define IS_QK_MOMENTARY(code)       IN_RANGE(code, QK_MOMENTARY, QK_MOMENTARY_MAX)
#define IS_QK_DEF_LAYER(code)       IN_RANGE(code, QK_DEF_LAYER, QK_DEF_LAYER_MAX)
#define IS_QK_TOGGLE_LAYER(code)    IN_RANGE(code, QK_TOGGLE_LAYER, QK_TOGGLE_LAYER_MAX)
#define IS_QK_ONE_SHOT_LAYER(code)  IN_RANGE(code, QK_ONE_SHOT_LAYER, QK_ONE_SHOT_LAYER_MAX)
#define IS_QK_ONE_SHOT_MOD(code)    IN_RANGE(code, QK_ONE_SHOT_MOD, QK_ONE_SHOT_MOD_MAX)
#define IS_QK_LAYER_TAP_TOGGLE(code) IN_RANGE(code, QK_LAYER_TAP_TOGGLE, QK_LAYER_TAP_TOGGLE_MAX)
#define IS_QK_TAP_DANCE(code)       IN_RANGE(code, QK_TAP_DANCE, QK_TAP_DANCE_MAX)
#define IS_QK_MACRO(code)           IN_RANGE(code, QK_MACRO, QK_MACRO_MAX)
#define IS_QK_KB(code)              IN_RANGE(code, QK_KB, QK_KB_MAX)
#define IS_QK_CAPS_WORD(code)       ((code) == QK_CAPS_WORD_TOGGLE)
#define IS_QK_LEADER(code)          ((code) == QK_LEADER)
```

#### `MO`

```c
#define MO(layer)   (QK_MOMENTARY | ((layer) & 0x1Fu))
```

---- keycodes that build on a layer, a modifier set or a number ----

layer while the key is down

```c
#define TO(layer)   (QK_TO | ((layer) & 0x1Fu))  // this layer only
#define TG(layer)   (QK_TOGGLE_LAYER | ((layer) & 0x1Fu))  // toggle a layer
#define DF(layer)   (QK_DEF_LAYER | ((layer) & 0x1Fu))  // set the default layer
#define OSL(layer)  (QK_ONE_SHOT_LAYER | ((layer) & 0x1Fu))  // layer for the next key
#define OSM(mods)   (QK_ONE_SHOT_MOD | ((mods) & 0x1Fu))  // modifiers for the next key
#define TT(layer)   (QK_LAYER_TAP_TOGGLE | ((layer) & 0x1Fu))  // momentary; tapped 5 times it toggles
#define TD(n)       (QK_TAP_DANCE | ((n) & 0xFFu))
#define LT(layer, kc) (QK_LAYER_TAP | (((layer) & 0xFu) << 8) | ((kc) & 0xFFu))
#define MT(mods, kc)  (QK_MOD_TAP | (((mods) & 0x1Fu) << 8) | ((kc) & 0xFFu))
#define LM(layer, mods) (QK_LAYER_MOD | (((layer) & 0xFu) << 5) | ((mods) & 0x1Fu))  // layer + modifiers while down
#define QK_LAYER_TAP_GET_LAYER(code) (((code) >> 8) & 0xFu)
#define QK_LAYER_TAP_GET_KEY(code)   ((code) & 0xFFu)
#define QK_MOD_TAP_GET_MODS(code)    (((code) >> 8) & 0x1Fu)
#define QK_MOD_TAP_GET_KEY(code)     ((code) & 0xFFu)
#define QK_LAYER_MOD_GET_LAYER(code) (((code) >> 5) & 0xFu)
#define QK_LAYER_MOD_GET_MODS(code)  ((code) & 0x1Fu)
#define QK_MODS_GET_MODS(code)       (((code) >> 8) & 0x1Fu)
#define QK_MODS_GET_KEY(code)        ((code) & 0xFFu)
```

#### `LCTL`

```c
#define LCTL(kc) ((MOD_LCTL << 8) | (kc))
```

A basic key with modifiers held around it: LSFT(KC_A) is shift + A. Same 5-bit mask as MOD_* below, in bits 8-12.

```c
#define LSFT(kc) ((MOD_LSFT << 8) | (kc))
#define LALT(kc) ((MOD_LALT << 8) | (kc))
#define LGUI(kc) ((MOD_LGUI << 8) | (kc))
#define RCTL(kc) ((MOD_RCTL << 8) | (kc))
#define RSFT(kc) ((MOD_RSFT << 8) | (kc))
#define RALT(kc) ((MOD_RALT << 8) | (kc))
#define RGUI(kc) ((MOD_RGUI << 8) | (kc))
```

### `core/keymap.h`

The keymap held in RAM: KEYMAP_LAYERS layers of MATRIX_ROWS x MATRIX_COLS keycodes, plus the two rotation keycodes of the encoder on each layer. It starts from the compiled-in default; store.h loads and saves it. The cfg fields of the lighting are held here in RAM too, but settings.h saves them (see keymap_cfg_set).

```c
#define KEYMAP_LAYERS 6
#define ENCODER_COUNT 1
```

#### `KEYMAP_MAC_LAYER`

```c
#define KEYMAP_MAC_LAYER    5
```

The two layers of the Mac side of the Win/Mac switch (board/os_switch.c): KEYMAP_MAC_LAYER is the base one (a copy of the base layer with Alt and GUI swapped) and KEYMAP_MAC_FN_LAYER is its own Fn layer, so the switch picks between two complete keyboards, each with a Fn layer, instead of just swapping two keys. Both are compiled in by the board's keymap_default() and editable in Vial like any other layer. Switching changes which layer the lookups fall back to; it does not touch what is stored.

```c
#define KEYMAP_MAC_FN_LAYER 4
```

```c

```

---- key overrides: a key with some modifiers held does something else, edited from Vial's Key Overrides tab ---- Vial's entry is 10 bytes: trigger keycode, replacement keycode, the layers it applies on (0xFFFF = all), the modifiers it needs, the ones that must not be held, the ones to take away while it acts, and the option bits (bit 7 = enabled). Kept as five words.

```c
#define KO_TRIGGER     0
#define KO_REPLACEMENT 1
#define KO_LAYERS      2
#define KO_MODS        3  // low byte: required, high byte: must-not-be-held
#define KO_ACTION      4  // low byte: suppressed, high byte: options
#define KO_FIELDS      5
#define KO_OPTIONS_ENABLED 0x80u
```

#### `KEYMAP_KEY_WORDS`

```c
#define KEYMAP_KEY_WORDS     ((uint16_t)(KEYMAP_LAYERS * MATRIX_ROWS * MATRIX_COLS))
```

---- the keymap as a run of 16-bit words, and the list of the words that changed ---- The store keeps the keymap in flash as a run of words in this order: the keys (layer, row, column), the encoders (layer, encoder, direction), the macros (two bytes a word, little-endian), the tap dances (index, field), the combos, the key overrides, the settings. A word is named by its offset in that run. Every edit notes the offset it changed, so that the store can write down just those words (a record of the log) instead of the whole keymap (four sector erases, ~130 ms of dark backlight).

```c
#define KEYMAP_ENCODER_WORDS ((uint16_t)(KEYMAP_LAYERS * ENCODER_COUNT * 2))
#define KEYMAP_MACRO_WORDS   ((uint16_t)(KEYMAP_MACRO_BYTES / 2))
#define KEYMAP_TD_WORDS      ((uint16_t)(KEYMAP_TAP_DANCE_COUNT * TD_FIELDS))
#define KEYMAP_COMBO_WORDS   ((uint16_t)(KEYMAP_COMBO_COUNT * COMBO_FIELDS))
#define KEYMAP_KO_WORDS      ((uint16_t)(KEYMAP_KEY_OVERRIDE_COUNT * KO_FIELDS))
#define KEYMAP_CFG_WORDS     ((uint16_t)KEYMAP_CFG_COUNT)
```

#### `KEYMAP_WORDS`

```c
#define KEYMAP_WORDS \
    ((uint16_t)(KEYMAP_KEY_WORDS + KEYMAP_ENCODER_WORDS + KEYMAP_MACRO_WORDS + KEYMAP_TD_WORDS + KEYMAP_COMBO_WORDS + KEYMAP_KO_WORDS + KEYMAP_CFG_WORDS))
```

### `core/layer.h`

Layer engine: a set of active layers on top of a default layer, the layer keycodes (MO, TO, TG, DF, OSL, TT, LM) and one-shot modifiers (OSM).

A key is looked up in the highest active layer that does not hold KC_TRANSPARENT; the default layer is tried last. The keycode found when a key goes down is the one used when it goes up (layer_key_down / layer_key_up), so a layer change between the two can never leave a key stuck.

### `core/leader.h`

Leader (QMK's): a key starts a sequence, and the keys pressed after it are not typed - they are matched against a table of sequences, and the one that matches acts. QMK keeps that table in the keymap too: it is written at compile time, not edited from Vial. Here it lives in board/leader.c.

The sequence abandons itself on a key that no sequence starts with, or after LEADER_TIMEOUT_MS of silence.

```c
#define LEADER_KEYS       6
#define LEADER_TIMEOUT_MS 400u
```

```c
    LEADER_NONE,   // no sequence starts like this
    LEADER_PREFIX, // a sequence starts like this: wait for more
    LEADER_MATCH,  // a whole sequence: act
} leader_match_t;
```

### `core/led.h`

The RGB backlight: a framebuffer of 8-bit levels, rendered from the effect of the profile in use, and the sequence of the 16 column subframes the hardware plays.

Every key has an RGB LED. A LED lights when its colour channel (a PWM output) is high AND the strobe line of its column is low, so the strobes of the key matrix are also the sinks of the LEDs: all the keys of one column (5 rows x R, G, B = 15 channels) are lit by one subframe, and a frame is 16 subframes interleaved with the key scans. The interrupt (board side) asks led_next_column() what to light and reads the levels; everything that takes time (the effects) is done in led_task() from the main loop, a few LEDs per pass, so that a repaint never holds up the keys.

```c
#define LED_ROWS     MATRIX_ROWS
#define LED_COLS     MATRIX_COLS
#define LED_CHANNELS (LED_ROWS * 3)  // per column: row 0 R G B, row 1 R G B, ...
```

#### `LED_DUTY1_BASE`

```c
#define LED_DUTY1_BASE 195u
```

The PWM channel n of a column has DUTY1 = LED_DUTY1_BASE + n (fixed, staggered like the stock firmware's so that the channels do not all switch at once) and DUTY2 = DUTY1 + width. The main loop keeps the DUTY2 values ready, so the timer interrupt only copies them.

#### `LED_WIDTH`

```c
#define LED_WIDTH(level) ((uint16_t)((uint16_t)(level) * 3u + ((uint16_t)(level) >> 1)))
```

8-bit level -> pulse width in PWM counts: 3.5 per step, 892 at most, so that DUTY2 stays below the 1200-count period

#### `LED_ANIM_FRAMES`

```c
#define LED_ANIM_FRAMES       9u
```

Frames (about 8 ms each) per step of the animation, and the lengths of the key flashes, in frames

```c
#define LED_RADIO_FLASH       62u  // ~0.5 s
#define LED_RADIO_PAIRING     1250u  // ~10 s of blinking
#define LED_RADIO_BLINK_HALF  30u  // half a period of that blink
#define LED_SPEED_MIN 1
#define LED_SPEED_MAX 16
#define LED_BRIGHTNESS_STEP 32
```

#### `LED_HUE_STEP`

```c
#define LED_HUE_STEP   16u
```

The colour of the plain effect, the way a picker means it: a hue (0-255) and a saturation (0 = white, 255 = the pure colour), packed into one setting - the hue in the low byte, the saturation in the high one. A colour picked in the Vial app is the colour that comes out, whatever it is. The lighting keys step the hue by LED_HUE_STEP and set full saturation, and land on white after the last hue.

```c
#define LED_SAT_FULL   255u
```

### `core/link.h`

Which way the keyboard talks to the host: the cable (USB), the 2.4 GHz dongle or Bluetooth. The mode selector on the board decides; in the two wireless positions the reports go to the radio (radio.h), in USB to the cable.

Bluetooth has three slots (three paired hosts). The keys B68_LK_1..3 choose one with a tap and start pairing with a 3-second hold. The slot in use is a setting that survives power-off (settings.h).

### `core/macro.h`

Vial macros: a macro key (M0, M1, ...) types a stored sequence. The buffer is the one Vial reads and writes (keymap_macro_*): macros back to back, each ended by a 0 byte. Plain characters are typed as on a US keyboard, and 0x01 introduces an action: tap / down / up of a key, a delay, or the same with a 16-bit keycode.

A macro does not stop the keyboard: macro_task() runs it one step per millisecond, so every report reaches the host before the next one, and a delay is a deadline, not a busy wait. Macros started while one runs wait their turn (up to MACRO_QUEUE of them).

```c
#define MACRO_QUEUE 4
```

### `core/matrix.h`

Matrix debounce and key events. Pure logic: no registers, so it runs under the host tests.

The board scans every column and hands the raw samples to matrix_feed(); a key change is accepted once that column has read the same value for MATRIX_DEBOUNCE_MS milliseconds, then queued as an event.

```c
#define MATRIX_ROWS 5
#define MATRIX_COLS 16
```

#### `MATRIX_DEBOUNCE_MS`

```c
#define MATRIX_DEBOUNCE_MS 5u
```

How long a column must hold a new value before it counts. It is a time and not a number of scans, as in QMK: the two knobs then move independently - the scan rate is free to follow the backlight's needs (core/sched.h) without the debounce paying for it. QMK's own default is 5 ms, and its choice of algorithm (sym_defer_pk) waits the same way.

#### `MATRIX_DEBOUNCE_SAMPLES`

```c
#define MATRIX_DEBOUNCE_SAMPLES 3u
```

A floor on how many scans must agree before a change counts. The time above is the rule; this only matters where the clock cannot be trusted to move (the simulator drives Timer 2 from a virtual flag), and at the real scan period of ~4 ms the time always comes first.

```c
#define MATRIX_ROW_MASK ((uint8_t)((1u << MATRIX_ROWS) - 1u))
```

#### `matrix_event_t`

```c
typedef struct {
    uint8_t col;
    uint8_t row;
    bool    pressed;
} matrix_event_t;
```

```c

```


raw[col] has bit `row` set for a pressed key; bits above the last row are ignored. A fresh scan of the whole matrix, with the time it was taken: `now` is what the debounce is measured against.

### `core/mouse.h`

Mouse keys (KC_MS_*): a pointing device that no other key of the keyboard needs. A direction held down moves the cursor in steps, faster the longer it is held (and faster again with MS_ACCEL1/2 held), a wheel key scrolls, and the buttons 1-5 hold their bit. The report is sent through core/report.c like the keyboard's, so the transport decides where it goes: USB has a mouse interface (REPORT_ID_MOUSE on interface 0, as the stock firmware had), the radio protocol has no mouse frame and drops it.

This is why the encoder can be a scroll wheel: assign MS_WH_UP / MS_WH_DOWN to its two directions in Vial and each detent scrolls once.

```c
#define MOUSE_REPEAT_MS 8u  // a step every 8 ms while a direction is held (the interval QMK uses)
#define MOUSE_ACCEL_MS  32u  // the step grows every 32 ms it is held...
#define MOUSE_STEP_MAX  8u  // ...up to this many units a step
#define MOUSE_WHEEL_MS  48u  // a wheel key held scrolls every 48 ms (a tapped one scrolls once)
```

### `core/override.h`

Key overrides: a key does something else while the right modifiers are held (Vial's Key Overrides tab edits them, core/keymap.c stores them). The entry is Vial's: a trigger keycode, a replacement, the layers it is active on (0xFFFF = all), the modifiers it needs, the ones that must not be down, the ones to take away while it acts, and the option bits (bit 7 = enabled).

Example: trigger Backspace, replacement Delete, required Shift -> Shift+Backspace deletes forward, and the Shift is still reported (unless it is also in "suppressed"). The trigger itself never reaches the host while the override acts; its release releases the replacement.

What is not implemented (none of them changes the everyday use): the QMK options about *when* the trigger activates (on the way down, or when the required modifiers arrive), "one modifier only", and the "do not re-register" variants. They are read and ignored.

### `core/radio.h`

The link to the BK3632 radio of the B68 (docs/keyboards/yunzii-b68-radio.md): a serial line at 260870 baud carrying frames [01][command][a][b][c][checksum] (the report is longer), a select line SEL that the MCU holds low while a frame goes out and releases with the last byte, and the radio's attention line ATT, high when the radio can take a frame and low while it is busy. This is how the stock firmware paces itself: a frame goes out only when ATT is high, and the answers (02 <command> ...) are not waited for. The radio's own frames are answered: 03 ... with F0, 08 ... with F1; without that it stays busy or refuses reports.

This file is the protocol and the scheduler, pure: the serial port and the pins are behind the radio_hook_* functions (board/radio_hw.c, or a test with a simulated radio).

```c
#define RADIO_MODE_2G4 0  // the "slot" of the mode command: 0 = 2.4G, 1-3 = Bluetooth
#define RADIO_MODE_BT3 3
#define RADIO_REPORT_LEN     30  // keyboard report frame
#define RADIO_COMMAND_LEN    6  // mode command, status request, acknowledgements
#define RADIO_CONSUMER_LEN   13
#define RADIO_NAME_FRAME_LEN 32
#define RADIO_NAME_MAX       24
#define RADIO_FRAME_MAX      32
```


#### `RADIO_STATUS_FLAGS_AT`

```c
#define RADIO_STATUS_FLAGS_AT      1u
```

What the status answer says. Six bytes after the command. Byte 1 carries the host's LEDs in bits 0-2 (num, caps, scroll); the stock firmware copies it to its LED state at 0x06B6. Bytes 4 and 5 are the **battery voltage as a 10-bit ADC reading**, little endian (byte 4 low, byte 5 the high two bits): the stock handler of the status frame (0x05EA-0x0690) builds XDATA[0x02E6..7] = byte5:byte4 and the gauge routine (0x7CF0) turns it into percent as (reading - 715) * 10 / 22, 0 below 715 and 100 above 935. It is *not* a 3-bit level (that was the NuPhy layout, and a wrong guess here). With the cable the reading saturates (0x03FF, 0x03FD ...), so it says nothing about the charge.

host LEDs in bits 0-2

```c

#define RADIO_STATUS_BATTERY_HI_AT 5u  // battery reading, high byte (0..3)
```

### `core/raw_hid.h`

The raw HID pipe VIA and Vial talk through: one 32-byte request on EP2 OUT, one 32-byte reply on EP2 IN.

One request is handled at a time. While one is being answered EP2 OUT is not armed, so the host's next packet is NAKed and retried: nothing is queued and nothing is lost. The interrupt only notes that a packet is there; the main loop reads it from the endpoint and answers it.


From the USB interrupt: a packet of `length` bytes arrived on EP2 OUT. One of another size is not a request of ours and is dropped. The interrupt copies nothing (32 bytes through a slow pointer held the timer interrupt up, and the backlight flickered while the HUD polled): the endpoint is not armed again until the request is answered, so its buffer stays as it is, and the main loop reads it from there.

### `core/report.h`

What the host is told: the keyboard state as a report, and the current consumer and system usages. This module only holds the state and builds the bytes; the transport (USB or radio) asks for them when keyboard.c says something changed (report_hook_send).

Two keyboard reports, and the host gets one of them at a time: the 112-bit NKRO one in report protocol (the chip's EP1 buffer is 16 bytes and the report ID takes one), and QMK's 8-byte six-key one in boot protocol (a BIOS has no idea what a bitmap is).

```c
#define REPORT_BOOT_SIZE 8  // mods, reserved, 6 keys
#define REPORT_BOOT_KEYS 6
```

#### `REPORT_NKRO_BITS`

```c
#define REPORT_NKRO_BITS  112
```

The NKRO report: the modifier byte, then one bit per usage from 0 to REPORT_NKRO_BITS - 1. QMK uses 120 bits (15 bytes), but this chip's EP1 buffer is 16 bytes and the report ID takes one of them: 112 bits (up to usage 0x6F, which covers the letters, the digits, the function keys and the navigation keys) makes the packet exactly 16 bytes.

```c
#define REPORT_NKRO_BYTES (REPORT_NKRO_BITS / 8)
#define REPORT_NKRO_SIZE  (1 + REPORT_NKRO_BYTES)
```

### `core/sched.h`

The timer interrupt plays two kinds of slots, one after the other: LED  - one column subframe of the backlight: the column stays lit for SCHED_LED_US, counted from the start of the slot SCAN - one scan of the key matrix, which takes as long as it takes (up to SCHED_SCAN_MAX_US) and is followed at once by the next slot After SCHED_SUBFRAMES_PER_SCAN LED slots comes a SCAN slot. The key lines and the LED sinks are the same lines, so the two can never overlap; that is what this sequence is for.

Every slot is timed from the start of its own interrupt, as the SMK port does: an LED slot is always a full SCHED_LED_US, whatever the scan before it took. (A fixed grid of slots cut the LED slot after a long scan short, and one column in five lit for a fraction of its time: a flicker.) So the frame of the backlight is not fixed: 16 LED slots and 2 scans, about 8 ms.

Why two scans and not four: a scan measured 753 us on the keyboard against a 500 us slot, so four per frame took a third of the CPU for the keys and left the main loop one pass between scans - a key press, which sends a radio frame, was enough to starve it and the backlight then stood aside. Halving the scans is half that load. The debounce is a time (MATRIX_DEBOUNCE_MS), so the keys do not pay for it.

The module counts time in timer counts (SCHED_COUNTS_PER_US per microsecond) and keeps the milliseconds from the time the interrupt says has really passed, so the clock does not depend on the lengths of the slots. It is pure: the timer and the hardware are in hal/tick.c and board/.

#### `slot_t`

```c
typedef enum {
    SLOT_LED,
    SLOT_SCAN,
} slot_t;
```

```c
#define SCHED_COUNTS_PER_US      2u  // the timer counts at FREQ_SYS / 12 = 2 MHz
#define SCHED_COUNTS_PER_MS      (1000u * SCHED_COUNTS_PER_US)
#define SCHED_LED_US             400u
#define SCHED_SCAN_MAX_US        1000u  // the timer is armed for this long during a scan, more than any scan takes; the interrupt then ends the slot itself
#define SCHED_SUBFRAMES_PER_SCAN 4u
```

#### `sched_slot_us`

```c
uint16_t sched_slot_us(slot_t slot);
```

The length the timer is armed for at the start of a slot

#### `sched_init`

```c
void sched_init(void);
```

#### `sched_step`

```c
slot_t sched_step(uint16_t elapsed, uint8_t *milliseconds);
```

At each interrupt: `elapsed` is the time that has passed, in timer counts, since the previous interrupt began. Returns the slot that starts now (what to do) and the number of whole milliseconds that have passed (usually 0 or 1; more only if a slot ran very long).

#### `sched_upcoming`

```c
slot_t sched_upcoming(void);
```

The slot after the one that started in the last sched_step(): the interrupt programs the timer for its length.

### `core/settings.h`

Settings that belong to the keyboard, not to the keymap: the sleep time, the Bluetooth slot and the lighting (effect, brightness, speed, colour - they live in the keymap's cfg fields in RAM, but are saved here: see keymap_cfg_set). A small record with a magic, a version and a CRC, written as a LOG in its own sector at 0xEC00: every save appends at the first erased slot and the last complete record wins. A save therefore never erases anything (no power cut can lose the previous settings, and the sector is erased once every SETTINGS_SLOTS saves instead of at each one). The profiles themselves are in store.h.

The sector after it (0xEE00) is left alone: the SMK port and the stock bootloader keep the "app bootable" marker there.

The flash is reached through the hooks of store.h (read, erase, program).

```c
#define SETTINGS_ADDR       0xEC00u  // the sector after the keymap store (0xEE00 holds the bootloader's marker: never touched)
#define SETTINGS_SECTOR     512u
#define SETTINGS_SLOTS      36u  // 14-byte records back to back in the sector
#define SETTINGS_QUIET_MS   500u  // changes are written once nothing has changed for this long and no key is down
#define SETTINGS_SLEEP_DEFAULT 2  // 10 minutes (the levels are listed in sleep.h)
```

### `core/sleep.h`

When the keyboard goes to sleep: after a time without use, or when asked. Pure logic; the sequence that puts the hardware to sleep is in board/sleep_hw.c.

The time without use is counted in seconds out of the millisecond clock of the main loop (a 16-bit clock wraps in 65 s, so this has to be called at least that often). The levels are the ones the keys Fn+O / Fn+P step through: 1, 5, 10, 30 minutes, never.

```c

#define SLEEP_LEVEL_DEFAULT 2  // 10 minutes
```

### `core/store.h`

The keymap in flash: one keyboard (keys, encoders, macros, tap dances, settings) in a pair of slots A/B of STORE_SLOT_SECTORS sectors; the RAM copy is in keymap.c. There used to be four profiles, which cost 16 KB of the chip's flash for a number of layouts nobody used: with one keyboard the store sits at the end of the flash and the code gets those bytes.

A whole save erases the slot that is NOT in use, writes the payload, and writes the header last. The header carries a sequence number and a CRC of the payload, so a slot only counts once it is complete; at load the valid slot with the newest sequence wins. A power cut during a save leaves the previous copy intact.

Most saves are not whole. The room left in a slot after the payload (about 340 bytes) is a LOG: an edit appends one five-byte record per changed word - no erase, so the backlight does not go dark and the flash is not worn - and the load puts the records over the payload. The whole save comes only when the log is full (about 69 words), when a lot changed at once (a reset, a macro) or when nothing was saved yet.

Flash map: code up to 0xDC00, the store (2 slots x 4 sectors of 512 bytes) at 0xDC00-0xEBFF, the settings at 0xEC00, the bootloader's marker at 0xEE00 (never touched), the stock bootloader at 0xF000.

```c
#define STORE_BASE         0xDC00u  // the code ends here
#define STORE_SECTOR_BYTES 512u
#define STORE_SLOT_SECTORS 4u
#define STORE_SLOTS        2u  // A and B, written alternately
#define STORE_END          (STORE_BASE + STORE_SLOTS * STORE_SLOT_SECTORS * STORE_SECTOR_BYTES)  // 0xEC00: the settings follow
```

#### `STORE_QUIET_MS`

```c
#define STORE_QUIET_MS 2000u
```

Edits are written once nothing has changed for this long and no key is down, so a flash write never lands in the middle of typing.

### `core/tapping.h`

Tap-or-hold keys: LT(layer, kc) and MT(mods, kc). Tapped, the key sends `kc`; held longer than the tapping term it switches the layer on or holds the modifiers.

TD(n) keys do the same with the five words of tap dance n (keymap_tap_dance_get): a tap sends "on tap", a hold longer than the term holds "on hold" (or "on tap" if that is empty), and when "on double tap" is set a second tap within the term sends it instead (a single tap then waits one term to be sure).

While such a key is undecided, the key events that follow are kept in a small queue and replayed once it is decided, so a key typed during the wait lands on the right layer (QMK does the same). No "permissive hold" or "hold on other key press": the decision is the release (tap) or the timeout (hold).

### `core/usb_desc.h`

The USB descriptors of the keyboard, as data.

Interface 0: HID boot keyboard on EP1 IN. Every report carries an ID (keyboard 3, system 1, consumer 2); in boot protocol

(a BIOS) the keyboard report goes out without it. A feature report (ID 5) takes the ISP command.

Interface 1: raw HID (usage page 0xFF60, as VIA and Vial expect) on EP2 IN + EP2 OUT, 32 bytes, no report IDs.

Windows keeps the descriptors it read for a VID:PID and bcdDevice: change USB_BCD_DEVICE whenever the interfaces, endpoints or report descriptors change.

```c
#define USB_VID        0x258Au  // the keyboard's own, so that sinowisp and Vial find it by the same ids as the SMK port
#define USB_PID        0xDEADu
#define USB_BCD_DEVICE 0x0203u  // 0203: the keyboard report is the NKRO bitmap now (Windows caches the descriptors on this)
#define USB_EP0_SIZE 8
#define USB_EP1_SIZE 16  // the chip's EP1 buffer; the NKRO report is exactly this big with its ID
#define RAW_HID_SIZE 32
```

#### `REPORT_ID_SYSTEM`

```c
#define REPORT_ID_SYSTEM   1
```

HID report IDs on interface 0

```c
#define REPORT_ID_CONSUMER 2
#define REPORT_ID_KEYBOARD 3
#define REPORT_ID_ISP      5
#define REPORT_ID_MOUSE    7  // as the stock firmware: 5 buttons, X and Y (16 bit), wheel
```

#### `USB_DESC_DEVICE`

```c
#define USB_DESC_DEVICE        1
```

Descriptor types

```c
#define USB_DESC_CONFIGURATION 2
#define USB_DESC_STRING        3
#define USB_DESC_HID           0x21
#define USB_DESC_HID_REPORT    0x22
#define USB_INTERFACES 2
```

#### `usb_desc_get`

```c
bool usb_desc_get(uint8_t type, uint8_t index, uint16_t wIndex, const uint8_t **data, uint16_t *length);
```

The descriptor for a GET_DESCRIPTOR request: `type` and `index` are the high and low byte of wValue, `wIndex` is the interface for the HID descriptors and the language for strings. False when there is no such descriptor.

### `core/usb_device.h`

The USB device on endpoint 0: enumeration and the HID class requests. Pure logic: the chip driver feeds it what arrives (a SETUP packet, an OUT packet, "the IN packet was taken") and it answers through the hooks below. It knows nothing of registers, so it runs under the host tests.

A control transfer, as the chip sees it: no data:  SETUP -> we arm an empty IN packet (status) -> its completion (usb_device_ep0_in_done) IN data:  SETUP -> IN packets of up to 8 bytes, each completion sends the next -> the host's empty OUT (status) OUT data: SETUP -> the host's OUT packet (usb_device_ep0_out) -> we arm an empty IN packet (status) -> its completion

```c
#define USB_SETUP_SIZE 8
```

#### `usb_hook_sof_ticks`

```c

```

Provided by the hardware: start-of-frame interrupts seen since power-on, wrapping. It stops counting when nothing drives the bus, which is what the cable being pulled out looks like. 16 bits: one start-of-frame a millisecond, an 8-bit counter came round exactly once in 256 ms, so a look at the bus that came 256 ms after the last one saw "no change" and declared the host gone (the backlight went off and the keys stopped).

SET_CONFIGURATION: endpoints in the initial state (toggles, stalls)

### `core/usb_reports.h`

From the report state to the packets on EP1. report_hook_send() (keyboard.c's way of saying "this changed") lands here: the packet is built from the report state right away and queued, and the main loop hands the queue to the endpoint one packet at a time as the host takes them. A key pressed and released in the same pass therefore still reaches the host as two reports.

Packets, by kind: keyboard = [ID 3] + modifiers and the NKRO bitmap, 16 bytes (in boot protocol the 8-byte six-key report, no ID), system = [ID 1, bits], consumer = [ID 2, usage lo, hi], mouse = [ID 7, buttons, x lo, x hi, y lo, y hi, wheel] (relative axes: the packet carries the movement accumulated until it was built). Consumer and system reports have no boot-protocol form: a BIOS gets the keyboard report only.

```c
#define USB_REPORT_QUEUE 8
```

### `core/via.h`

via_receive() takes one request and rewrites the same buffer into the reply, which the transport sends back as it is, like QMK's raw_hid_receive(). A command this firmware does not implement answers with 0xFF in the first byte ("unhandled").

### `core/vialrgb.h`

The Lighting tab of the Vial app (docs/vial.md): the app's effect list, brightness, speed and colour, driving the effects this keyboard has.

The app decides whether to show the tab from the keyboard *definition* (the field "lighting": "vialrgb" in board/vial.json) and then asks the firmware which effects it has. This firmware has its own effects, not QMK's rgb_matrix, so the ids of the six that have a counterpart are offered and mapped onto them (core/vialrgb.c); the colour is one of the seventeen the effects use.

## Board (`board/`)

The B68 itself: pins, the matrix, LEDs, the radio's serial port, sleep, the keycodes of the board, and the glue that implements the hooks of `core/`.

### `board/b68_keys.h`

#### `B68_HUD_TOG`

```c
#define B68_HUD_TOG 0x7E00u
```

Keycodes specific to the B68: the first QK_KB values, in the order the Vial definition lists them under customKeycodes. They are numbered from 0x7E00 with no gap (check_vial.py enforces it), so removing one from the middle renumbers the ones after it: the four profile keys went when the profiles did.

```c
#define B68_FX_PREV 0x7E01u  // lighting effect - / +
#define B68_FX_NEXT 0x7E02u
#define B68_BRI_DN  0x7E03u  // brightness - / +
#define B68_BRI_UP  0x7E04u
#define B68_SPD_DN  0x7E05u  // effect speed - / +
#define B68_SPD_UP  0x7E06u
#define B68_COL_DN  0x7E07u  // colour of the plain effect - / +
#define B68_COL_UP  0x7E08u
#define B68_LK_1    0x7E09u  // Bluetooth slot 1-3: a tap selects it, held for 3 s it starts pairing
#define B68_LK_2    0x7E0Au
#define B68_LK_3    0x7E0Bu
#define B68_BATTERY 0x7E0Cu  // shows the battery level on the number keys (it was the radio trace in the SMK port, which Oblio does not have)
#define B68_SLEEP   0x7E0Du  // sleeps now, only in the wireless modes
#define B68_SLP_DN  0x7E0Eu  // inactivity time before sleep: shorter / longer
#define B68_SLP_UP  0x7E0Fu
#define B68_LEADER  0x7E10u  // starts a Leader sequence (the sequences are in board/leader.c)
```

### `board/isp.h`

#### `isp_jump`

```c

```

Jumps to the stock bootloader's ISP mode (at 0xFF00), the way `sinowisp` flashes the keyboard. Never returns. Interrupts are switched off first; call it from the main loop, not from an interrupt: the bootloader never executes RETI, so an interrupt left in service would stay that way.

### `board/led_hw.h`

The backlight on the chip: the PWM channels P1.3-5 / P2.0-5 / P3.0-5 as colour sources, the column strobes as sinks.

A subframe lights the keys of one column: the previous column goes off, the 15 pulse widths of this column are loaded, the strobe of the column goes low and the PWM outputs are enabled last, so the column lights at once. A column with nothing to show is left dark.

#### `led_hw_init`

```c
void led_hw_init(void);
```

#### `led_hw_enable`

```c
void led_hw_enable(bool on);
```

Whether the backlight is allowed to light: it is not while the keyboard waits for the USB host to enumerate it (a bus-powered device must stay within 100 mA until configured) or while the bus is suspended. A wake from sleep re-initialises the channels and with them this permission (led_hw_init), so the caller has to look at led_hw_enabled() and ask again.

#### `led_hw_enabled`

```c
bool led_hw_enabled(void);
```


### `board/os_switch.h`

The Win/Mac switch of the B68. It is not in the key matrix: it is P0.5, an input with a pull-up that the stock firmware samples all the time, debounces with two counters (ten equal readings in a row) and keeps in XDATA[0x0307] (function at 0xA9D9 of the dump). Every keymap lookup of the stock then goes through that state, so the switch picks which of its two sets of keymap tables is the base: the same idea as here, where it picks between two complete keyboards - layers 0/1 on Windows, layers KEYMAP_MAC_LAYER/KEYMAP_MAC_FN_LAYER on Mac, the second pair being a copy of the first with Alt and GUI swapped and its own Fn layer, both editable in Vial.

Measured on the board (with a port readout, since removed, 2026-11-01): P0.5 reads HIGH with the switch on Mac and LOW with it on Windows, and the level does not depend on the column strobes (it is not wired into the matrix). The two captures alone could not tell which position was which; the keyboard did, when the layer came out on the wrong side.

```c
#define OS_SWITCH_STABLE_MS 50u  // the switch must read the same this long before the layer changes, as the mode selector
```

### `board/radio_hw.h`

The serial port and the pins of the link to the BK3632 radio: TXD = P5.5, RXD = P5.6 (EUART0), SEL = P0.2 (an output of the MCU, low while a frame goes out), ATT = P4.7 (an input: high = the radio can take a frame).

The handler is declared here because SDCC builds the vector table from the module that defines main(): main.c must include this header.

#### `radio_uart_isr`

```c

```

INT_EUART0


### `board/stage.h`

Bring-up stage (see the Makefile): how much of the firmware is started. The code is the same in every stage; a lower stage leaves the later parts alone, so that a fault on the first runs on the hardware is found in the module that brought it. 1  matrix, USB, Vial, HUD, profiles, settings, encoder 2  + the backlight (PWM outputs, the timer's LED slots) 3  + the radio, the mode selector and the Bluetooth keys 4  + sleep: the release build

```c
#    define OBLIO_STAGE 4
#define STAGE_LED   (OBLIO_STAGE >= 2)
#define STAGE_RADIO (OBLIO_STAGE >= 3)
#define STAGE_SLEEP (OBLIO_STAGE >= 4)
```
